investigations.title: Observe and count dividing cells
investigations.question: Which visible features support a phase classification, and what can phase counts tell us?
investigations.sourceKind: authentic textbook mitosis micrographs (Fig. 16.8), with separately labelled synthetic counts

variables.compare: cell phases in the same specified tissue region
variables.observe: visible chromosome arrangement and assigned phase
variables.holdConstant: sampling field boundaries and classification rules

investigations.prediction: Predict which visible feature would distinguish metaphase from anaphase before opening the annotated comparison.
procedure: Inspect the authentic supplied Fig. 16.8 micrographs at full size; record the cell label, visible chromosome feature and tentative phase before revealing the reference. Do not claim these are verified onion cells or that the synthetic counts were measured from these selected photos.
Compare your classifications with the annotated reference, retaining ambiguous cells as uncertain.
Use the separate illustrative 100-cell table to compute the mitotic index. Estimate phase times only under the supplied asynchronous, steady-population model and 20-hour cycle assumption.
Explain how field choice, ambiguous boundaries and unequal cell-cycle conditions affect the inference.
investigations.expected: Illustrative mitotic index is (12+6+4+6)/100 = 0.28 = 28%. Model phase times are 14.4, 2.4, 1.2, 0.8 and 1.2 hours, summing to 20. A photograph supports digital observation, not slide preparation or physical microscope competence.
limitations: Selected micrographs illustrate phases; they are not an unbiased field for estimating phase frequencies.
Phase frequencies approximate time only under stated model assumptions.

investigations.title: Expected ratios and observed offspring
investigations.question: How closely do simulated Aa × Aa offspring match the predicted ratio in different samples?
investigations.sourceKind: synthetic independent offspring samples under a stated complete-dominance model

variables.holdConstant: parental genotypes, equal gamete probabilities, independent unions, equal survival

investigations.prediction: Construct the gametes and expected probabilities before examining the samples. Predict whether each group must equal 1:2:1 exactly.
procedure: Construct Aa × Aa and record AA=1/4, Aa=1/2, aa=1/4, with phenotype assumptions stated.
Calculate expected counts for 10 and 100 offspring. Record differences between observed and expected.
Compare replicate samples at the same size before comparing small and large samples.
Revise a claim that one deviation proves an inheritance rule false; state what patterns and additional evidence would justify a different model.
investigations.expected: Expected counts are 2.5,5,2.5 at n=10 and 25,50,25 at n=100; expected counts need not be whole observed organisms. Samples vary by chance. The supplied large samples show smaller proportional departures than the most uneven small sample, but this is not guaranteed for every draw.
limitations: Simulation does not demonstrate breeding or field data collection.
No tongue rolling, earlobes or private family traits are treated as simple Mendelian tests.

investigations.title: Test a DNA sequence explanation
investigations.question: Can sequence and fragment evidence distinguish an insertion from a substitution?
investigations.sourceKind: authored DNA/fragment model, with fictional labels

variables.observe: coding sequence, translated segment and predicted fragment sizes
variables.holdConstant: 5′→3′ coding orientation, reading frame, standard supplied codon table, the supplied separate fragment-assay model

investigations.prediction: Predict whether an unchanged fragment pattern guarantees an unchanged DNA sequence.
procedure: Transcribe each coding sequence using the stated orientation, then translate complete codons with the supplied code table.
Compare reference and substitution products; do not assume every substitution changes an amino acid.
Compute total fragment sizes and interpret the one-base insertion while retaining a practical gel-resolution limitation.
Design an additional sequence-based test that could distinguish equal-length molecules. Respond to the alternative claim that a matching gel proves identity.
investigations.expected: Reference mRNA AUG GAA UUU UAA yields Met–Glu–Phe then stop. Substitution AUG GAG UUU UAA gives the same peptide. Insertion AUG AGA AUU UUA plus one incomplete base alters the displayed reading frame; a downstream stop is not shown. Totals are 1000,1000,1001 bp. A typical classroom gel may not resolve a one-base difference near these sizes; sequencing would be more discriminating.
limitations: Fragments are a separate simplified assay model and are not calculated from the short displayed coding segment.
Matching bands establish compatibility at tested sites, not personal identity or guilt.
investigations.collaborationEvidence: Independent planning, comparison and revision are observable here. Live teamwork and physical laboratory performance are not certified.
